title: God gave the increase (1 Corinthians 3:5–9)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the foolishness of the cross, and a mocking drawing on a Roman wall. Your line was foolish and wise. What foolish kindness did you do? Day five hundred seventy.

Remember Apollos? Eighteen days ago, Priscilla and Aquila took him aside in Ephesus and taught him the way of God more perfectly. Then he crossed to Achaia, Corinth's province, and Acts says he was a great help to the believers there. By the time Paul writes this letter, the church in Corinth has split into fan clubs. Some say, I'm with Paul. Some say, I'm with Apollos. Others, I'm with Cephas, that is, Peter. And some, I'm with Christ. Parishes, teams and families still split this way over favorite people.
screen: `APOLLOS COMES TO CORINTH.` → `I'M WITH PAUL. I'M WITH APOLLOS.` → `A CHURCH OF FAN CLUBS.`

segments.voice: Paul could have used this moment to win. He was the founder, after all. Instead he deflates the whole contest, including himself. Who is Paul, and who is Apollos? he asks. Servants, through whom you believed, each doing what the Lord gave him. Then the picture, in the Douay-Rheims, which spells the name Apollo: "I have planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the increase." A farmer's image. Paul put the seed in the ground in Corinth. Apollos came along later with the watering can. Both mattered. But neither of them can make a seed grow. Growth is not something you can do to a plant; you can only set things up and wait. So, Paul says: "Therefore, neither he that planteth is any thing, nor he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase." That's humbling for the famous preacher, and freeing for everyone else. Then he adds: he who plants and he who waters are one, and each will receive his own reward according to his own labor. Then he widens the picture: "For we are God's coadjutors: you are God's husbandry; you are God's building." Coadjutors means co-workers. Husbandry here means a farm, a field under cultivation. The Corinthians aren't anyone's fan club. They're God's field. Notice how gently Paul treats Apollos. Not a rival, a co-worker. And notice the honest limit of every worker's job. You can't make your kids believe, your friend heal, your project take off, or your parish grow. You plant, you water, and the increase belongs to God. It's a line Catholics reach for when their part seems small.
screen: `WHO IS PAUL? WHO IS APOLLOS?` · `ONE PLANTS, ONE WATERS.` · `ONLY GOD MAKES IT GROW.` · `GOD'S CO-WORKERS.` · then, large: `GOD GAVE THE INCREASE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do your small part. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you care about that you can't control: a child's faith, a friend's recovery, a project at work, a parish, a garden. What's your part in it today? Planting, watering, or simply not trampling it? Name that one small part. Then picture yourself setting down the rest, the growing, which was never yours to do. See if the weight of it lifts a little. If you pray, you can hand God the increase, and keep only your watering can. The bell holds the time.
God gave the increase. Paul planted, Apollos watered, and neither could make anything grow: the growth belongs to God. Today's word.
Your line: god gives the increase. Today, do your one small part well, and let go of the outcome. Day five hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Catholics speak of many vocations and gifts serving one Church, priests, religious, catechists, parents and parishioners each with a part, and they pray for growth that they believe comes from God alone.

original.note: Greek: made it grow, gave the increase. the verb is kept for God alone.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about teamwork.
what it means: Paul ends a church's fan-club quarrel by saying every worker is a servant, and only God makes anything grow.

what a scholar hears: Paul uses tenses carefully: planted and watered are single past acts, but God was giving the increase all along. and synergoi, co-workers, is the word the Douay-Rheims renders coadjutors.

Editor review (2026-10-01): 1 Corinthians 3:6, 3:7 and 3:9 now quoted from the Douay-Rheims (which spells Apollo and says 'coadjutors'), not the KJV. Hook: 'preached so brilliantly that' the church split was an unsourced causal claim (now Acts 18:27's help to the believers); dropped 'rather smugly'; Peter named as Cephas per 1:12; no longer tells the listener 'knows the feeling'. Cut the synergy etymology (repeated day 566). Douay wording checked against drbo.org.
